title: Bhadda Kapilani
hook: Kassapa's wife parts from him at a crossroads, later becomes a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns in remembering past lives (AN 1.14; Therigatha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, calling the council, and your line: so it isn't lost. Did you share one thing worth keeping? Today we go back to the woman who walked out of the house beside Kassapa, and follow her. Day seven hundred forty-five.

He takes the road to the right. She takes the road to the left. That's the whole parting, as the commentary tells it. Two people in simple robes had been walking one behind the other since they left their great house. A few days back we heard how Pippali and Bhadda married as friends and left home together. Then, at a crossroads, they stop. People who see them pass might think they're still a couple, and that could cloud the life they've chosen. So at the fork they go separate ways. We followed him for most of a week. Today is about her.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON ONE ROAD.` → `A FORK AHEAD.` → `RIGHT FOR HIM, LEFT FOR HER.`

segments.voice: First, the parting. In the commentary it's done with respect, not regret. They've shared a house and a friendship. Now each one walks toward the same goal by a separate road. Second, the waiting. When Bhadda left, the commentary says, there was not yet an order of nuns. So she waited, and lived the homeless life as best she could. Later, when women were ordained, she was ordained among them, and in time she reached the goal. Third, her gift. In the list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Bhadda Kapilani foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Not foremost because of her husband. In her own right, in her own line of the list. Fourth, her own verses. In the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Bhadda speaks. She begins by praising Kassapa: the Buddha's true heir, who knows his former lives and has reached the end. And then she turns, and says the same of herself. She too has that knowledge. She too has come to the end. They both saw the misery of the world, she says, and went forth. Both are now freed, at peace. Notice what she does. She doesn't make herself smaller to praise him, and she doesn't make him smaller to claim her place. She stands beside him in the poem the way she walked beside him out of the house. Then she walks her own road. Her own path.
screen: `A PARTING WITH RESPECT.` · `SHE WAITED FOR AN ORDER OF NUNS.` · `FOREMOST IN HER OWN RIGHT.` · `HER VERSES STAND BESIDE HIS.` · then, large: `HER OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a partner's path. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you're close to: a spouse, a partner, a sibling, a best friend. Think of a road they walk that isn't yours. A faith, a calling, a sport, a craft, a grief. Something you don't share, and maybe don't fully understand. Don't try to join it or fix it. Just picture them on that road, and wish them well on it. Then let the picture rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bhadda Kapilani. Kassapa's wife, who parted from him at a crossroads, became a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Today's word.
Your line: her own path. Today, ask someone close to you one real question about the road they walk that you don't, and listen to the answer all the way through. Day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Bhadda Kapilani among the great nuns of the Buddha's time, and her verses are read with the other elder nuns' poems in the Therigatha.

fork.setup: you're Bhadda, walking behind the man you left home with. people might mistake you for a couple still. what do you do?
options: part at the crossroads and take your own road.
fork.reveal: at the crossroads he goes right and she goes left; later she is ordained and reaches the goal in her own right.

original.note: Pali pubbenivasa, former lives: remembering them is the gift for which Bhadda is named foremost among the nuns.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wife in Kassapa's story.
what it means: a nun who walked her own road and is named foremost in her own right.
what a scholar hears: AN 1.14 names her foremost among nuns in recalling past lives, and her verses in the Therigatha praise Kassapa and then claim the same attainment for herself.

notes: All paraphrased; Mrs. Rhys Davids's Psalms of the Sisters (1909) is public domain, but the writer was not certain of its exact wording.
Crossroads story is commentarial: confirm the reason given (people might think wrongly of them), right for him and left for her. Embellishments (the earth trembling) left out.

Her waiting: the commentary has her stay among other (non-Buddhist) women ascetics until Mahapajapati's order existed; the script says only that she waited and 'lived the homeless life as best she could'. Confirm framing; no length of time given.

Therigatha verses paraphrased: praise of Kassapa as son and heir, knower of former lives and of heaven and hell, ended birth; then 'Bhadda Kapilani' claims the same; both saw the world's peril, went forth, are freed and cooled. Confirm.
'Pubbenivasa' as the gift in AN 1.14: confirm the Pali term used there.
'A few days back' refers to day 739 in this path.
Editor: the hook now opens on the parting itself instead of another road scene (days 740 and 744 also open on the road); fixed the garbled original note ('named foremost in among the nuns').
